ssrSchedulingComparison.method: Local adaptation of measure-ssr-arrivals.mjs. In the control only, transpile render-scheduler.ts from the control commit using workspace TypeScript ES2022/ESNext into render-scheduler.js. Select the before/after adapter through the benchmark worker import. Preserve all other host, renderer and load-driver code. Source maps are not used for measurement. Verify participant and adapter hashes before and after every case. Final full-distribution controls retain the pre-extraction render-policy.js from c8711bfa, while changed adapters use 8a766808 including the shared work window. All final comparisons share the server build from 8a766808.
ssrSchedulingComparison.nodePrototype: Uncommitted diagnostic clone of Node admission.js. Give its checkpoint a streaming capability using Bun createBunRenderPolicy(gate, enqueue).streaming only while the Node gate shouldSchedule() is true. Initial admission and buffered rendering retain their existing behavior. That prototype precedes the committed shared work-window implementation. Final Node comparisons substitute only admission.js from c8711bfa for the before case, retaining the shared server build in both variants.

loadDriverCalibration.conclusion: Rust has substantially more static-response generation capacity and lower driver CPU at scheduled demand. Actual SSR pilot throughput fell for both participants with Rust. Matching headers and a concurrency-32 connection-reuse check passed, but these controls do not explain the workload-dependent difference. Keep Rust opt-in. Do not infer framework improvement from a changed generator.

The temporary copied Rust variant adds a one-millisecond Tokio sleep before every request, including warmup. Not accepted as a driver behavior change.
methodology.writeObservation: React only, three-second warmup and seven-second measurement. Temporary socket handle wrappers time native write calls and observe Node streamBaseState asynchronous-write indicator immediately after return.
methodology.cpuProfiles: React only, Node then Rust in one worker. Inspector profiles include three-second warmup, five-second measurement and control setup. Sample attribution uses wall-clock deltas, not precise thread CPU.
methodology.syscallTrace: React only, Node then Rust in one worker, two-second warmup and five-second measurement. strace 6.19, seccomp filter, writev only, raw arguments, timestamps and syscall duration. Tracing materially changes throughput and cannot establish untraced write cost.

metricBoundaries.validRps: Sum of two per-driver measured-stage validRps. Their start times differ slightly, so this is not an exactly common-window throughput estimator.
metricBoundaries.cpuPerResponse: Probe process CPU delta divided by probe request count, including warmup, measurement and small control traffic.
metricBoundaries.requestsPerTurn: Probe requests divided by setImmediate observer turns, a coarse batching observation rather than a complete event-loop model.
metricBoundaries.nativeWriteMicroseconds: Probe elapsed wall time inside each native socket write wrapper. Includes Node native preparation and kernel time. Not isolated syscall CPU.

conclusions: Keeping the worker alive and reversing driver order reproduces the sustained-concurrency slowdown. Worker CPU remains roughly saturated while CPU per response rises with Rust, especially for React.
Core isolation does not remove the React difference. Both drivers reuse 64 connections and produce approximately one request per socket read.
At 4,000 offered requests/second, both drivers complete approximately 4,000 valid responses/second with no errors. The large CPU-per-response difference does not persist at this demand.
A one-millisecond refill sleep does not recover Node throughput. All observed server socket writes complete synchronously with both drivers. Increased asynchronous write backpressure is unsupported.

Instrumented native write calls take longer under Rust saturation, but syscall tracing reduces both drivers to approximately 2,900 requests/second and removes the gap. Its syscall timings cannot explain untraced behavior.

No framework or driver correctness defect is confirmed. A faster static-response driver is not interchangeable in a sustained-concurrency framework measurement. The larger eXact/React ratio is not evidence of a framework optimization.
openFrontier: The causal interaction among closed-loop request timing, V8 string work, kernel loopback costs and host scheduling remains unresolved. CPU profiles and probe timings locate differences but do not identify a safe code optimization.

The original pacing, profiling and socket controls cover Node buffered preloaded SSR only. No corresponding causal conclusion is established for streamed SSR, normal service fetching, Bun, Deno, workerd or a remote driver.

bunBufferedControl.methodology: One resident native Bun fetch worker per framework, preloaded buffered SSR and bounded telemetry. Two fresh drivers, concurrency 32 each, per block. Three-second discarded warmup and seven-second measurement. Driver order Node, Rust, Rust, Node. Worker telemetry sampled every 500 ms. No listener or socket probe. Short uncontrolled-host diagnostic, not an accepted framework baseline. Temporary coordinator remains outside Git, so the SHA alone does not reproduce the diagnostic.
conclusions: The slowdown also appears in native Bun buffered preloaded SSR. React is approximately 31% slower and eXact approximately 4% slower with Rust in this short control. Both driver orders agree in direction. All measured requests validate with zero errors.
The effect cannot be attributed solely to Node HTTP server write handling, since this control uses Bun native fetch serving. The exact shared mechanism remains unresolved.
The smaller eXact difference is preliminary on an uncontrolled host. These short runs do not establish a new framework performance baseline or results for streaming or normal data loading.

refillDelayExperiment.scope: Targeted preloaded buffered SSR diagnosis on an uncontrolled host. Temporary copied driver and coordinator source remain outside Git. The repository SHA alone does not reconstruct these variants. No production source change or accepted baseline replacement.

methodology.nodeGap: Copied Node driver records full-response completion timestamp to next dispatch in the same logical request slot, including validation, histogram work and promise handoff. Two drivers at concurrency 32 each, React, native Node and Bun, three-second warmup and five-second measurement. This is not a fixed event-loop sleep. Driver instrumentation can add small overhead.
methodology.timedVariant: A temporary copy of the existing Rust driver delays refill after completed responses. The first request in each logical slot is not delayed. One reusable nonblocking Linux timerfd per delayed slot is driven by Tokio AsyncFd, with no busy spinning or per-request timer fd allocation. Delay histograms measure elapsed time across timer arm and async wake. Slots share the normal connection pool, so this is a refill delay rather than an enforced minimum idle interval on each individual TCP connection.
methodology.sweep: React only. Two drivers at concurrency 1, 8, 32 or 64 each, total concurrency 2, 16, 64 or 128. Node control and Rust delays 0, 20, 100 and 1,000 microseconds. Two-second discarded warmup and three-second measurement. Two populations reverse runtime, concurrency and variant order. A resident native worker per runtime/population, preloaded data and bounded telemetry.
methodology.confirmation: React only, total concurrency 64. Node control, Rust 0, 1 and 20 microseconds, and Tokio yield_now without a timed wait. Three-second discarded warmup and five-second measurement. Two reversed populations with fresh drivers and resident workers.
methodology.exactControl: eXact, total concurrency 64, Rust 0 and 20 microseconds, Node and native Bun. Three-second discarded warmup and five-second measurement, two reversed populations.
methodology.metrics: RPS sums measured-stage validRps from the two drivers, whose starts differ slightly. CPU per response uses whole warmup plus measurement worker telemetry deltas. Timed delay means are weighted by observation count across both drivers. Percentiles are retained as per-driver ranges rather than pooled quantiles.

conclusions: The initially measured Node completion-to-refill gap at total concurrency 64 has a per-driver median of 14 to 15 microseconds and mean of 17 to 19 microseconds. This varies with workload and concurrency. The 10 ms event-loop monitor sampling interval must not be interpreted as a per-request delay.

React sweep: the requested 20-microsecond delay improves mean Rust throughput at total concurrency 16, 64 and 128 on both runtimes, but individual Bun results vary. At total concurrency 2 it reduces Node throughput and leaves Bun throughput approximately unchanged. Larger delays impose a severe low-concurrency penalty.

React confirmation at total concurrency 64: Rust 0 to 20 microseconds improves mean valid throughput from 6,564 to 8,079 requests/second on Node (23%) and 6,989 to 7,979 on Bun (14%). Both reversed-order confirmation runs improve, with substantial differences in gain size. Node driver controls remain faster.

The requested 20-microsecond timer produces substantially longer observed waits, around 40 to 60 microseconds in typical high-concurrency cases. Report requested and observed delays separately. The 1-microsecond timer produces roughly 9-microsecond waits in the confirmation.

Plain Tokio yield_now has no consistent comparable benefit. The 1-microsecond timed wait is also less effective than the 20-microsecond wait. This supports timing sensitivity without proving a unique cause.

The eXact selected-delay control does not show a clear throughput gain. No default delay or framework change is justified. All warmup and measured requests in the retained captures validate with zero errors.
openFrontier: No sharp universal failure threshold was established. The shape depends on runtime, concurrency and renderer. Delay gains do not prove socket exhaustion or excessive keep-alive reuse.

Timed waiting adds timer syscalls, epoll events and wakeups as well as elapsed idle time. A yield control does not isolate all those effects, so the causal kernel/runtime mechanism remains unresolved.
No validation covers streamed SSR, normal service fetching, remote drivers, other frameworks, Deno or workerd. These generator experiments are not framework optimizations.
